title: Block close: find your way
hook: many doors into prayer, all opening to the same house
tomorrow: Love, and do what you will

segments.voice: Yesterday, journaling and prayer walks: prayers on paper and on foot. Your line was pray as you walk. Which house did you write down? Day one thousand one hundred eighty-one.

Luke has already shown Jesus slipping away into the wilderness to pray, and once spending all night in prayer on a mountain. His disciples have been watching. Then one day, Luke says, "as he was praying in a certain place, when he ceased," one of them asks: "Lord, teach us to pray." Not teach us about prayer. Teach us to do it. For this whole block of the path, we've been walking through a house of prayer, room after room, each one furnished by a different family of Christians. Today the block closes. There's no new room. There's a question, and it's a practical one. Of all the doors you've opened, which one will you keep using?

Walk back through the rooms. The Benedictines: listen, the hours, the kitchen rota, tools treated like altar vessels. The Orthodox way of the heart: the mind brought down into the heart, watchfulness at the door, the prayer rope. The Franciscans, with brother and sister creatures. The Carmelites, with Teresa's four ways to water a garden and God among the pots and pans. The Ignatian way: imagine the scene, notice consolation and desolation. The Celtic blessings for everything. Anglican morning and evening prayer. Luther's advice to his barber, Reformed psalms and family worship. Anabaptist yieldedness, Quaker silence, Methodist class meetings, a covenant renewed. And lately, louder rooms: hands raised in praise, a hand on a shoulder, a word weighed, bold prayer for the sick, the preacher calling and the people answering, testimony, a Taizé line sung over and over, Iona's prayers for justice, a shared table, a notebook and a walk. One thing is worth saying plainly. None of these was invented as a sampler. Each belongs to a community and a whole life of faith, and is meant to be kept, not tried once. Benedict asked his monks to promise stability: stay put, and let the place shape you. In John's Gospel, Jesus uses a word with the same patience in it: "Abide in me, and I in you." Abide means stay, remain, keep living there. And when the disciples asked to be taught, Luke records no catalog of methods. Jesus said, "When ye pray, say, Our Father which art in heaven," one prayer to keep. So this block ends with a choice. Not the best way. Your way, for now. One door you'll walk through every day this month, until it feels like a room you live in.

Here's the practice: choose one way to keep this month. Settle, and breathe. Let the rooms of this block drift past, without judging them. A chant. Silence. A prayer rope. A walk. A psalm at bedtime. A journal. Notice which one you keep coming back to. Choose that one. Then make it small and concrete: when, where, and for how long. Five minutes is plenty. If you pray, you can offer the choice to God. The bell holds the time.
Block close. The end of the block on traditions of prayer: many rooms walked through, and one way chosen to keep.

Your line: one way, kept. Today, write down the way you chose and the time you'll keep it, and do it once before you sleep. Tomorrow a new block begins: living it. Day one thousand one hundred eighty-one.

howItsDone: In Christian practice, a rule of prayer is something kept over time: a daily office, a rosary or prayer rope, a quiet time with the Bible, a weekly prayer meeting, sometimes with guidance from a pastor, priest or spiritual director.

Benedict's vow of stability (Rule ch. 58) paraphrased as 'stay put, and let the place shape you'; confirm.
howItsDone describes a rule of prayer as something kept over time, with examples from several traditions; confirm.
'Five minutes is plenty' in the practice is advice, not a claim about a tradition.
